intro.why: How a model is served and rolled out decides its latency, cost and blast radius when something goes wrong; and ML, LLM and agent systems each need different operational metrics.

sections.title: The model inference function
sections.plain: A prediction is a fixed function of the input features and the trained model.
sections.body:
$$\text{prediction}=f(\text{input features},\ \text{trained model})$$

At inference time the model is fixed: no learning happens, only computation. Example:

def predict_species(features):
    processed = preprocess(features)
    return model.predict(processed)

predict_species((5.1, 3.5, 1.4, 0.2))   # → "Iris-setosa"

sections.title: Feature encoding and training-serving consistency
sections.plain: Turn raw inputs into the exact same numbers at training and at serving time.
sections.body:
Feature encoding converts raw, often non-numerical inputs into a numerical feature vector (e.g. raw measurements → [5.1, 3.5, 1.4, 0.2]; categories → one-hot columns).

Rule: the encoding code used in training and inference must be identical. Put it in a shared, reusable library; otherwise you get training-serving skew: the model receives vectors it was never trained on, and nothing crashes.

Code example ex1: re-implementing a one-hot encoder with a different category order changed a basic-plan customer's churn probability from 0.977 to 0.416 with no error.

sections.title: Four designs for serving a model
sections.plain: Embed it, call it, run it over the data, or look up precomputed answers.
sections.body:
DesignHowExample
1. LibraryModel embedded in the application; a local function callTesseract OCR in a desktop app
2. Service / cloud serviceA dedicated server exposes REST; replicated across VMs or containersThe iris FastAPI service
3. Batch processingMove the model to the data; score everything on a scheduleNightly streaming recommendations
4. Cached predictionsPrecompute or memoise and look upTranslations of common words; a film's age rating classified once ("Frozen" → U)

In ex1, an LRU cache answered 98.5% of 50,000 requests without calling the model.

sections.title: Basic and ramped deployments
sections.plain: Update everything at once, or one server at a time.
sections.body:
"Hot" (zero-downtime) strategies aim to update without users noticing: basic, ramped, blue/green and canary.

Basic: all nodes updated at once. Not outage-proof, slow rollback; only for tiny applications.

Ramped (rolling, incremental): replace one node at a time; the default in Kubernetes. Pros: easy rollback, less risky. Cons: both versions must be supported simultaneously (API and data compatibility), and verification is slow.

sections.title: Blue/green and canary deployments
sections.plain: Switch between two identical environments, or try the new version on a few users first.
sections.body:
Blue/green: v2 is released into a second, identical environment alongside v1; after QA/UAT there, traffic is switched over. Pros: simple, fast, instant rollback (switch back). Cons: cost of a duplicate environment (especially with many microservices); tests may miss issues, and all traffic shifts at once. (Which colour denotes staging and which production varies between teams.)

Canary: release to a small subset of users first, then roll out fully if metrics stay healthy (e.g. a social network enabling a feature in one region first).

StrategyDowntimeRollbackBlast radiusCost
BasicYesSlowEveryoneLow
RampedNoEasyGrowingLow
Blue/greenNoInstantEveryone at switchHigh (2×)
CanaryNoFastSmall subsetMedium (routing)

sections.title: End-to-end MLOps simulation
sections.plain: Data → validation → features → training → registry → deployment → monitoring → drift → retraining.
sections.body:
Diabetes-style MLOps simulator
  1. Data simulation: synthetic data with the Pima diabetes schema, configurable size and drift.
  2. Validation and EDA.
  3. Feature engineering.
  4. Training.
  5. Evaluation and model registry.
  6. Deployment: simulated Docker/Kubernetes rollout (rolling, blue/green or canary).
  7. Monitoring: latency, throughput, errors.
  8. Drift and retraining: when the population stability index exceeds a threshold, retrain and redeploy.
$$\text{PSI}=\sum_{i}(a_i-e_i)\,\ln\frac{a_i}{e_i}$$

$e_i$, $a_i$: expected (training) and actual (live) share of observations in bin $i$. Common thresholds: below 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.2 moderate, above 0.2 significant. Code example ex2 runs the loop: PSI rises from 0.008 to 0.48 as glucose drifts, triggering retraining. Notice that live AUC barely moved: input drift does not always hurt accuracy, so many teams combine PSI with performance checks before retraining.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Feature stores solve training-serving skew systematically: one definition, offline and online materialisations.
  • Shadow + canary combine well: shadow first for correctness at zero risk, canary for real-user behaviour.
  • LLM costs scale with tokens: caching, smaller models for easy requests and prompt compression are operational levers.
  • Agent runs need traces: log every thought, tool call and result so failures can be replayed.

code.title: Inference function, encoding skew and cached predictions
code.explain: The same customer gets 0.977 with the shared encoder and 0.416 with a re-implemented one; an LRU cache then serves 98.5% of 50,000 requests without calling the model.
mistakes: Copy-pasting feature code into the serving service.
Caching predictions whose inputs change continuously.
code.notes: Package encode() in a versioned library imported by both training and serving.
code.code:
"""Prediction = f(input features, trained model), and why encoding must be shared.

A churn model is trained with one-hot encoded 'plan'. A serving team re-implements
the encoding with a different category order: predictions silently change
(training-serving skew). Importing the same encode() fixes it. Finally, cached
predictions turn repeated requests into dictionary lookups.
"""
import numpy as np
from functools import lru_cache
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

PLANS = ["basic", "standard", "premium"]
def encode(plan: str, monthly_spend: float, tenure_months: int) -> np.ndarray:   # shared library
    onehot = [1.0 if plan == p else 0.0 for p in PLANS]
    return np.array(onehot + [monthly_spend / 100, tenure_months / 12])

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
rows = [(rng.choice(PLANS, p=[.5, .3, .2]), rng.uniform(10, 120), int(rng.integers(1, 60))) for _ in range(3000)]
X = np.array([encode(*r) for r in rows])
y = np.array([int((r[0] == "basic") * 1.5 - r[2] / 24 + rng.normal(0, .6) > 0) for r in rows])
model = LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)                      # fixed at inference time

def predict_churn(plan, spend, tenure):                     # the inference function
    return float(model.predict_proba(encode(plan, spend, tenure).reshape(1, -1))[0, 1])

SERVING_PLANS = ["premium", "standard", "basic"]            # re-implemented elsewhere, different order
def encode_reimplemented(plan, spend, tenure):
    return np.array([1.0 if plan == p else 0.0 for p in SERVING_PLANS] + [spend / 100, tenure / 12])

print(f"{'request':<26} {'shared encode':>14} {'re-implemented':>15}")
for req in [("basic", 30.0, 3), ("premium", 90.0, 40), ("standard", 50.0, 12)]:
    good = predict_churn(*req)
    bad = float(model.predict_proba(encode_reimplemented(*req).reshape(1, -1))[0, 1])
    print(f"{str(req):<26} {good:14.3f} {bad:15.3f}{'   <- skew' if abs(good - bad) > .1 else ''}")

@lru_cache(maxsize=10_000)                                   # cached predictions design
def cached(plan, spend_bucket, tenure):
    return predict_churn(plan, spend_bucket * 10.0, tenure)
reqs = [(rng.choice(PLANS), int(rng.integers(1, 12)), int(rng.integers(1, 24))) for _ in range(50_000)]
for r in reqs: cached(*r)
info = cached.cache_info()
print(f"\ncached predictions: {info.hits:,} hits / {info.misses:,} model calls for {len(reqs):,} requests "
      f"(hit rate {info.hits / len(reqs):.1%})")

code.title: MLOps loop with PSI drift detection
code.explain: Simulates weekly batches with increasing glucose drift, computes PSI against training data, and retrains and re-registers when PSI > 0.2.
mistakes: Retraining on drift alone when performance is fine.
Recomputing reference bins on live data.
code.notes: In production, drift tools (Evidently, WhyLabs) compute PSI/KS per feature and alert.
code.code:
"""A compressed end-to-end MLOps loop on synthetic diabetes-style data.

simulate -> validate -> features -> train -> evaluate & register -> deploy -> monitor
-> drift check (PSI) -> retrain when PSI exceeds 0.2. Glucose drifts upward over
weeks; the monitor detects it and the loop retrains and redeploys.
"""
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
def simulate(n, shift=0.0):                                   # 01 data simulation (Pima-like schema)
    glucose = rng.normal(120 + shift, 30, n); bmi = rng.normal(32, 6, n); age = rng.normal(33, 11, n).clip(21, 81)
    z = 0.045 * (glucose - 120 - 0.6 * shift) + 0.09 * (bmi - 32) + 0.03 * (age - 33) - 0.6
    y = (z + rng.normal(0, 1, n) > 0).astype(int)
    return np.c_[glucose, bmi, age], y

def validate(X):                                              # 02 validation
    assert not np.isnan(X).any() and (X[:, 0] > 0).all(), "invalid batch"
    return X

def psi(expected, actual, bins=10):                           # population stability index
    edges = np.quantile(expected, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)); edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    e = np.histogram(expected, edges)[0] / len(expected); a = np.histogram(actual, edges)[0] / len(actual)
    e, a = np.clip(e, 1e-4, None), np.clip(a, 1e-4, None)
    return float(np.sum((a - e) * np.log(a / e)))

registry, version = [], 0
def train_and_register(X, y):                                 # 03-05 features, train, evaluate, register
    global version
    m = LogisticRegression(max_iter=500).fit(X, y); version += 1
    registry.append({"version": version, "auc": roc_auc_score(y, m.predict_proba(X)[:, 1])})
    return m

Xtr, ytr = simulate(3000); ref_glucose = Xtr[:, 0]
model = train_and_register(validate(Xtr), ytr)
print(f"deploy v{version} (canary 10% -> 100%)")              # 06 deployment
for week, shift in enumerate([0, 5, 12, 22, 35], start=1):    # 07-08 monitoring and drift
    Xw, yw = simulate(1500, shift); validate(Xw)
    p = psi(ref_glucose, Xw[:, 0]); auc = roc_auc_score(yw, model.predict_proba(Xw)[:, 1])
    status = "OK" if p < 0.1 else ("WARN" if p < 0.2 else "DRIFT -> retrain")
    print(f"week {week}: glucose mean {Xw[:, 0].mean():6.1f}  PSI {p:5.3f}  live AUC {auc:.3f}  serving v{version}  {status}")
    if p >= 0.2:
        Xnew = np.r_[Xtr[-1500:], Xw]; ynew = np.r_[ytr[-1500:], yw]
        model = train_and_register(Xnew, ynew); ref_glucose = Xnew[:, 0]
        print(f"        retrained -> registered v{version}, rolling update")
print("registry:", [(r["version"], round(r["auc"], 3)) for r in registry])
